p.src: Now Kongming released Meng Huo and all his companions, granted official ranks and titles to Yang Feng and his sons, and richly rewarded their cave troops. Yang Feng and the others bowed their thanks and departed. Meng Huo and his companions fled through the night back to Silver Pit Cave. Outside the cave were three rivers: the Lu River, the Gannan River, and the Xicheng River. As the three waterways converged, the place was called Three Rivers. For more than three hundred li north of the cave, the land was nearly level and yielded all manner of produce. Two hundred li west of the cave was a salt well. Two hundred li to the southwest, the way led directly to Lu and Gan. Three hundred li due south lay Liangdu Cave, where mountains encircled and embraced the settlement; the mountains produced silver ore and were therefore called the Silver Pit Mountains. Palaces, halls, and towers had been built among the mountains to serve as the barbarian king's stronghold. Within it stood an ancestral temple called the “Household Ghost.” In every season they slaughtered oxen and horses as sacrificial offerings, a rite they called “Divining the Ghost.” Each year they regularly sacrificed people from Shu together with outsiders. When anyone fell ill, they refused medicine and prayed only to shamans, calling this the “Medicine Ghost.” There were no penal laws in that land; anyone who committed a crime was simply beheaded. When girls came of age, they bathed in the streams; men and women mingled freely and chose their own mates without parental restraint, a custom called “Learning the Art.” When the year's rainfall came in due measure, they planted rice and grain; but if the crops failed, they killed snakes for stew and cooked elephants for food. In each district, the foremost household was styled “Cave Lord,” and the next in rank “Chieftain.” On the first and fifteenth days of every month, everyone traded and exchanged goods in Three Rivers City. Such were the customs of that land.

p.src: Now Meng Huo gathered more than a thousand clansmen in the cave and told them, “Again and again I have suffered humiliation at the hands of the Shu army, and I have sworn to avenge it. What wise counsel have you to offer?” Before he had finished, one man answered, “I can recommend a man who will defeat Zhuge Liang.” The company looked and saw Meng Huo's wife's younger brother, presently chief of the Eight Tribes, known as Cave Lord Dailai. Meng Huo was delighted and eagerly asked who the man was. Cave Lord Dailai said, “Southwest of here lies Bana Cave. Its lord, King Mulu, is deeply versed in magic: when he goes abroad he rides an elephant, can summon wind and rain, and is always followed by tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, venomous snakes, and vicious scorpions. He also commands thirty thousand spirit soldiers, all exceedingly valiant. Your Majesty should write him a letter and prepare gifts; I shall personally go and seek his aid. If he consents, what need have we to fear the Shu army?” Meng Huo gladly ordered his brother-in-law to take a letter and depart. He then ordered King Duosi to guard Three Rivers City as the forward bulwark.

p.src: Now Kongming led his army straight to Three Rivers City and saw from afar that water bordered it on three sides, while only one side opened onto dry land; he therefore sent Wei Yan and Zhao Yun with a force to assault the city from the landward side. When the troops reached the walls, bows and crossbows loosed together from above. The cave dwellers were mostly trained in archery, and each crossbow discharged ten bolts at once, every head smeared with poison; whoever was struck saw his flesh rot away until his entrails showed, and died. Unable to prevail, Zhao Yun and Wei Yan returned to Kongming and reported the poisoned arrows. Kongming himself rode his small carriage to the front to examine the true situation, then returned to camp and ordered the army to withdraw several li and pitch camp. Seeing the Shu army retreat far away, the southern soldiers laughed and congratulated one another, believing that fear alone had driven the enemy back. Thus they slept soundly that night and sent out no scouts.

p.src: Now after Kongming had ordered the retreat, he shut the gates of his camp and did not come forth. For five days running, he issued no commands. Toward dusk, a light breeze suddenly arose. Kongming gave the order: “Every soldier must have a piece of his garment ready for inspection by the first watch. Anyone without one will be beheaded at once.” None of the generals understood his purpose, but the soldiers made ready as ordered. At the first watch another order came: “Every soldier is to wrap one bundle of earth in his piece of cloth. Anyone without one will be beheaded at once.” Again the soldiers did not understand his purpose, but could only prepare as commanded. Kongming then ordered: “All troops are to deliver their bundles of earth beneath the walls of Three Rivers City. Those who arrive first will be rewarded.” On hearing the order, the soldiers all wrapped clean earth and raced toward the city walls. Kongming ordered them to heap the earth into a scaling ramp and proclaimed that the first man onto the wall would win the highest merit. Thereupon more than a hundred thousand Shu troops and over ten thousand surrendered soldiers cast all their bundled earth beneath the walls at once. In an instant the piled earth became a hill reaching to the top of the walls. At a single secret signal, the Shu troops all swarmed onto the walls. When the southern soldiers hastened to discharge their crossbows, more than half had already been seized; the rest abandoned the city and fled. King Duosi died amid the chaos of battle. The Shu commanders led their troops along separate routes to pursue and destroy the enemy. Having taken Three Rivers City, Kongming distributed all the captured treasures among the army. The beaten remnants of the southern army escaped back to Meng Huo and reported, “King Duosi has been killed. Three Rivers City is lost.” Meng Huo was greatly alarmed.

p.src: While he was anxiously considering the matter, a man reported that the Shu army had already crossed the river and was now encamped before his own cave. Meng Huo fell into a great panic. Suddenly someone came out laughing from behind a screen and said, “How can a man be so devoid of wit? Though I am only a woman, I am willing to go out and fight beside you.” Meng Huo looked and saw that it was his wife, Lady Zhurong. The Lady's family had dwelt in the southern lands for generations, and she was a descendant of the clan of Zhurong; she was skilled with throwing knives and never missed her mark. Meng Huo rose and thanked her. The Lady gladly mounted her horse and led several hundred fierce officers of her clan and fifty thousand fresh cave troops out of the Silver Pit palace to confront the Shu army. She had just rounded the cave entrance when a body of troops blocked her way, led by the Shu general Zhang Ni. At the sight, the southern troops swiftly deployed in two wings. Lady Zhurong had five throwing knives at her back, held an eighteen-foot spear in her hand, and rode a curly-haired Red Hare horse. Zhang Ni saw her and privately marveled. The two spurred their horses and clashed. After only a few bouts, the Lady wheeled her horse and fled. Zhang Ni gave chase, and a throwing knife came dropping through the air. He hastily raised a hand to ward it off, but it struck him squarely in the left arm, and he tumbled from his horse. With a great shout, the southern soldiers seized and bound Zhang Ni and carried him away. When Ma Zhong heard that Zhang Ni had been captured, he hastened out to rescue him, but the southern soldiers had already laid a trap. Seeing Lady Zhurong rein in her horse and stand with spear leveled, Ma Zhong charged her in fury, but his mount was tripped and he too was captured. Both prisoners were escorted into the cave and brought before Meng Huo. Meng Huo laid a feast to celebrate. The Lady ordered the executioners to drag Zhang Ni and Ma Zhong out and behead them. Meng Huo stopped her, saying, “Zhuge Liang has released me five times. If we kill his generals now, it would be unrighteous. Imprison them in the cave for now. It will not be too late to kill them after we have captured Zhuge Liang.” The Lady accepted his words, and they drank, laughed, and made merry.

p.src: Now the defeated remnants came before Kongming and told him what had happened. Kongming at once summoned Ma Dai, Zhao Yun, and Wei Yan, gave each his secret instructions, and sent them forth with their own forces. The next day, southern soldiers reported inside the cave that Zhao Yun had come to challenge them. Lady Zhurong immediately mounted and rode out to meet him. Wei Yan next led a force forward to challenge her, and the Lady spurred her horse out to meet him. Just as the fighting grew fierce, Wei Yan feigned defeat and fled, but the Lady refused to pursue. The following day, Zhao Yun again led a force to challenge her, and the Lady brought out her cave troops to meet him. After a few bouts, Zhao Yun feigned defeat and fled, but the Lady held her spear still and did not pursue. As she was about to withdraw her troops to the cave, Wei Yan led his men in shouting insults at her. Enraged, the Lady leveled her spear and charged Wei Yan. Wei Yan wheeled his horse and fled. The Lady pursued in fury, while Wei Yan galloped into a narrow and secluded mountain path. Suddenly there came a loud crash behind him. Wei Yan turned and saw the Lady falling backward from her saddle: Ma Dai had been lying in ambush there and had tripped her horse with a rope. They seized and bound her on the spot and escorted her back to the main camp. When the southern officers and cave troops came to her rescue, Zhao Yun charged and scattered them in a single attack.

p.src: Kongming sat upright in his tent. When Ma Dai brought Lady Zhurong in under guard, Kongming at once ordered the warriors to unbind her, invited her to a separate tent, and gave her wine to calm her nerves. He then sent a messenger to tell Meng Huo that he wished to exchange the lady for the two generals Zhang Yi and Ma Zhong. Meng Huo agreed, immediately released Zhang Yi and Ma Zhong, and returned them to Kongming. Kongming then sent the lady back into the cave. Meng Huo received her, at once delighted and vexed. Suddenly, word came that the lord of Bana Cave had arrived. Meng Huo went out of the cave to welcome him and saw the man riding a white elephant, his body adorned with gold and pearl necklaces and two great swords hanging at his waist. Escorted by a band of men who tended tigers, leopards, jackals, and wolves, he entered amid their throng. Meng Huo bowed twice and pleaded piteously, recounting all that had happened. King Mulu promised to avenge him. Meng Huo was overjoyed and held a banquet in his honor. The next day, King Mulu led out the troops of his cave together with his ferocious beasts. When Zhao Yun and Wei Yan learned that the southern troops had emerged, they drew up their forces in battle formation. The two generals reined up side by side before the lines and looked on. The banners and weapons of the southern army were unlike any others: most of the men wore neither clothes nor armor but stood entirely naked, their faces hideous; each bore four pointed knives; no drums or horns sounded in their army, for they used the striking of gongs as their signal; King Mulu, with two precious swords at his waist and a handbell in his hand, rode forth on a white elephant from beneath the great standard. At the sight, Zhao Yun said to Wei Yan, “We have spent our lives upon the battlefield, yet never have we seen such a man.” While the two were still pondering, King Mulu muttered some unknown incantation and shook the bell in his hand. Suddenly a violent wind arose, whipping sand and stones through the air like a driving rain; at one blast of a painted horn, tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, venomous snakes, and savage beasts came forth upon the wind, baring fangs and brandishing claws as they charged. How could the Shu soldiers withstand them? They fell back at once. The southern troops pursued and slaughtered them, turning back only after driving them as far as the road on the border of the Three Rivers.

Kongming laughed loudly. “How could such a petty trick as yours deceive me? Twice before, men of your own caves captured you and brought you to submit, and I did you no harm. You imagined that I now trusted you completely, so you came feigning surrender, intending to kill me inside the cave!” He ordered the warriors to search them, and sure enough, each man carried a sharp knife. Kongming asked Meng Huo, “You said that only if you were captured in your own home would you be truly convinced. What say you today?” Meng Huo replied, “We came of our own accord to seek death; this was no feat of yours. I am not convinced.” Kongming said, “I have captured you six times, yet still you will not submit. How long do you intend to wait?” Meng Huo replied, “If you capture me a seventh time, then I shall submit to you with all my heart and swear never to rebel again.” Kongming said, “Your lair is already broken. What have I to fear?” He ordered the warriors to unbind them all, then rebuked them: “If I capture you this time and you equivocate again, I shall show no mercy!” Meng Huo and the others fled away in abject terror.

Kongming then ordered the gate guards to admit them all.
The lord of Dailai Cave led in axemen escorting Meng Huo and several hundred others, and bowed below the hall.
Kongming shouted, “Seize them for me!”
The strong soldiers rushed out from both corridors. Two men seized each enemy, and all were bound and taken prisoner.
Kongming laughed loudly. “How could such a petty trick as yours deceive me?
Twice before, men of your own caves captured you and brought you to submit, and I did you no harm.
You imagined that I now trusted you completely, so you came feigning surrender, intending to kill me inside the cave!”
He ordered the warriors to search them, and sure enough, each man carried a sharp knife.
Kongming asked Meng Huo, “You said that only if you were captured in your own home would you be truly convinced.
What say you today?”
Meng Huo replied, “We came of our own accord to seek death; this was no feat of yours.
I am not convinced.”
Kongming said, “I have captured you six times, yet still you will not submit. How long do you intend to wait?”
Meng Huo replied, “If you capture me a seventh time, then I shall submit to you with all my heart and swear never to rebel again.”
Kongming said, “Your lair is already broken. What have I to fear?”
He ordered the warriors to unbind them all, then rebuked them: “If I capture you this time and you equivocate again, I shall show no mercy!”
Meng Huo and the others fled away in abject terror.

p.src: Now more than a thousand battered survivors of the southern army were fleeing, most of them wounded, when they encountered King Meng Huo. Meng Huo gathered the defeated troops and felt somewhat heartened. He then consulted the lord of Dailai Cave: “My cave stronghold has now been occupied by the Shu army. Where can we go to find refuge?” The lord of Dailai Cave replied, “There is only one kingdom capable of defeating Shu.” Delighted, Meng Huo asked, “Where can we go?” The lord of Dailai Cave replied, “Seven hundred li southeast of here lies a kingdom called Wuge. Its ruler, Wutugu, stands twelve feet tall. He eats no grain but feeds upon live snakes and savage beasts; his body is covered in scales that neither blades nor arrows can penetrate. All the soldiers under his command wear rattan armor. The rattan grows in mountain ravines, twining over walls of stone. The people gather it and soak it in oil, taking it out only after half a year to dry in the sun. Once dry, it is soaked again. Only after this has been repeated more than ten times is it fashioned into armor. When worn, it does not sink while crossing rivers, does not become wet in water, and admits neither blade nor arrow. For this reason, they are called the Rattan-Armored Army. Your Majesty may now go and seek his aid. If you obtain his help, capturing Zhuge Liang will be as easy as a sharp blade splitting bamboo.” Meng Huo was overjoyed and set off for Wuge to seek an audience with Wutugu. There were no houses in his cave domain; all the people dwelt in earthen burrows. Meng Huo entered the cave, bowed twice, and piteously recounted all that had happened. Wutugu said, “I shall raise the troops of my cave and avenge you.” Meng Huo gladly bowed in thanks. Wutugu then summoned two commanders: one named Tu’an and the other Xini. He raised thirty thousand soldiers, all clad in rattan armor, and marched northeast from Wuge. They came to a river called Peach Blossom Water. Peach trees grew along both banks, and year after year their fallen leaves accumulated in the stream. If people from another country drank its water, they invariably died; only the people of Wuge could drink it, and it doubled their vigor. Wutugu’s army reached the Peach Blossom ford and encamped there to await the Shu forces.

p.src: Now Kongming sent local scouts to learn Meng Huo's movements. They returned and reported, “Meng Huo has invited the ruler of Wuge to lead thirty thousand rattan-armored troops, who are now encamped at the Peach Blossom Ford. Meng Huo is also gathering tribal warriors from every quarter to unite their strength against us.” On hearing this, Kongming advanced with his army straight to the Peach Blossom Ford. p.src: The next day, the ruler of Wuge led a formidable force of rattan-armored troops across the river, with gongs and drums resounding thunderously. Wei Yan led his troops out to meet them. The tribal warriors swept forward like a storm across the ground. The Shu soldiers shot crossbow bolts at their rattan armor, but none could pierce it, and all fell to the ground; neither sword strokes nor spear thrusts could penetrate it. The tribal troops wielded sharp blades and steel forks; unable to withstand them, the Shu soldiers fled in utter defeat. The tribal troops did not pursue, but turned back. Wei Yan returned and pursued them to the Peach Blossom Ford, where he saw the tribal troops crossing the water in their armor; those who were exhausted removed their armor, laid it upon the water, and crossed seated on top of it. Wei Yan hurried back to the main camp and reported every detail to Kongming. Kongming summoned Lü Kai and the local people and questioned them. Lü Kai said, “I have long heard that among the southern tribes there is a land called Wuge, whose people know nothing of civilized relations. They also protect themselves with rattan armor, making them difficult to wound at short notice. There is also the poisonous peach-leaf water, which actually invigorates the people of that country when they drink it; but people from other lands die as soon as they drink it. Even if we completely conquered such a savage region, what benefit would it bring? We would do better to withdraw the army and return at once.” Kongming laughed. “I did not come all this way with ease. How could I simply leave? Tomorrow I shall have a plan to subdue them.” He then ordered Zhao Yun to help Wei Yan guard the camp and warned them not to venture out rashly.

p.src: The next day, guided by a local man, Kongming rode in his small carriage to a secluded mountainous place on the north bank of the Peach Blossom Ford and surveyed the terrain everywhere. Where the mountains were perilous and the ridges steep, the carriage could go no farther, so Kongming left it and continued on foot. Suddenly he came to a mountain and saw a valley shaped like a long serpent. On every side were sheer, bare walls of rock without a single tree, and through the middle ran a broad road. Kongming asked his guide, “What is this valley called?” The man replied, “This place is called Coiled Serpent Valley. Beyond the valley lies the main road to Sanjiang City, and the land before the valley is called Talang Plain.” Kongming was overjoyed. “Heaven has bestowed this place upon me so that I may succeed!” He retraced his route, mounted his carriage, and returned to camp. Summoning Ma Dai, he instructed him: “I shall give you ten black, oil-coated wagons, and you will need a thousand bamboo poles. As for what is to be placed inside the wagons, arrange it thus and thus. Take the troops under your command and secure both ends of Coiled Serpent Valley, then carry out my instructions exactly. I give you half a month to have everything ready. When the appointed time comes, deploy everything in this fashion. If anyone escapes, you will assuredly be punished under military law.” Ma Dai received the plan and departed. Kongming next summoned Zhao Yun and instructed him: “Go beyond Coiled Serpent Valley and guard the junction of the Sanjiang road in this manner. Have everything required ready by the appointed day.” Zhao Yun received the plan and departed. Kongming then summoned Wei Yan and instructed him: “Lead your own troops to the Peach Blossom Ford and make camp there. If the tribal troops cross the water to attack, abandon the camp and flee toward the place where you see a white flag. Within half a month, you must lose fifteen successive engagements and abandon seven stockades. If you lose only fourteen, do not come back to see me.” Wei Yan accepted the order, but was displeased at heart and departed in dejection. Kongming also summoned Zhang Yi and ordered him to lead a separate force to the appointed place and construct a stockade; then he commanded Zhang Yi and Ma Zhong to take the thousand surrendered men from the local caves and act according to his instructions. Each of them carried out the plan.

p.src: Meanwhile, Meng Huo said to Wutugu, ruler of Wuge, “Zhuge Liang has many cunning schemes, but they amount to little more than ambushes. In future engagements, instruct the whole army not to advance rashly whenever they see thick woods in the valleys.” Wutugu replied, “Your Majesty speaks wisely. I already know that the people of the Central Plains are much given to deceitful stratagems. Henceforth I shall act according to your counsel. I shall fight in the vanguard; you remain in the rear and direct me.” The two settled their plans. Suddenly word came that the Shu army had established a camp on the north bank of the Peach Blossom Ford. Wutugu at once sent two tribal chiefs to lead the rattan-armored troops across the river and engage the Shu army. After only a few exchanges, Wei Yan fled in defeat. Fearing an ambush, the tribal troops did not pursue but returned of their own accord. The next day, Wei Yan went out and set up camp once more. The tribal scouts discovered this, and their army again crossed the river to give battle. Wei Yan went out to meet them. After only a few exchanges, he fled in defeat. The tribal troops pursued for more than ten li. Seeing no movement anywhere around them, they occupied the Shu camp. The next day, the two tribal chiefs invited Wutugu to the camp and informed him of what had happened. Wutugu immediately led his army forward in force and pursued Wei Yan for a time. The Shu troops cast aside armor and weapons as they fled, until they saw a white flag ahead. Wei Yan led his defeated troops swiftly to the white flag, where a stockade had already been built, and took up quarters within it. Wutugu drove his troops after them; when he arrived, Wei Yan led his men out, abandoning the camp once more. The tribal troops captured the Shu camp. The next day, they continued the pursuit. Wei Yan turned back to fight, but was defeated again in fewer than three exchanges. He fled toward the white flag and found another stockade, where he and his troops took up quarters. The next day, the tribal troops arrived once more. Wei Yan fought briefly, then fled again. The tribal troops occupied the Shu camp.

p.src: To avoid a tedious account, Wei Yan fought and retreated until he had lost fifteen battles and abandoned seven camps in succession. The tribal troops advanced in force, pressing the pursuit. Wutugu himself led the army in routing the enemy, but whenever he encountered a place along the road where trees grew thickly, he dared not advance; instead, he sent men to observe from a distance, and sure enough they saw banners fluttering among the shadows of the trees. Wutugu said to Meng Huo, “Everything is just as Your Majesty foresaw.” Meng Huo laughed heartily. “This time I have seen through Zhuge Liang's scheme! For days Your Majesty has defeated him in fifteen battles and seized seven camps, while the Shu troops flee at the mere sight of you. Zhuge Liang has exhausted his stratagems; one more advance, and the great matter will be settled!” Wutugu was delighted and thereafter gave no further thought to the Shu army.

p.src: On the sixteenth day, Wei Yan led his battered remnant out to face the rattan-armored troops. Wutugu rode foremost upon an elephant, wearing a cap adorned with the sun and moon and fringed with wolf whiskers, and golden beads and tassels about his body. Scaly armor showed beneath his ribs, a faint gleam shone in his eyes, and he pointed at Wei Yan and reviled him. Wei Yan wheeled his horse and fled. The southern troops surged forward behind him. Wei Yan led his men around Coiled Serpent Valley and fled toward a white banner. Wutugu commanded his host in pursuit, cutting down all within reach. Seeing no trees or grass upon the hills, Wutugu judged that no ambush could be concealed there and pursued without misgiving. Upon reaching the valley, he saw several dozen carts bearing black, oil-coated chests blocking the road. A southern soldier reported, “This is the route by which the Shu army transports its provisions. When Your Majesty’s troops arrived, they abandoned their supply carts and fled.” Wutugu was delighted and urged his troops onward in pursuit. As they were about to emerge from the valley, no Shu troops could be seen; instead, timbers and rocks came tumbling down in confusion and piled up to seal the valley mouth. Wutugu ordered his men to clear a path and advance, when suddenly they saw carts large and small ahead, all laden with dry firewood, burst into flame. Wutugu hurriedly ordered a retreat, but cries arose from the rear ranks reporting that the valley entrance had already been barricaded with dry wood and that the carts had all been packed with gunpowder, which was now ablaze at once. Since he saw no vegetation about, Wutugu was not yet alarmed and ordered his men to seek another way out. Then torches were hurled down from both sides of the mountain. Wherever they landed, powder fuses buried in the ground caught fire, and iron bombs erupted from the earth. Flames danced wildly throughout the valley, and every suit of rattan armor they touched caught fire. Wutugu and his thirty thousand rattan-armored troops burned as they clutched one another and perished in Coiled Serpent Valley. Looking down from the mountain, Kongming saw the southern troops flailing their limbs as the fire consumed them, while most had their heads and faces shattered by the iron bombs. All lay dead in the valley, and the stench was unbearable. Kongming shed tears and sighed, “Though I have rendered service to the state, this deed will surely shorten my life!” All the officers and soldiers around him sighed with emotion.

p.src: Kongming returned to camp, took his seat in the command tent, and told his generals, “I resorted to this stratagem only because I had no choice, but it has gravely diminished my store of hidden virtue. I knew the enemy would expect me to place ambushes where the woods were thick, so I merely displayed banners there and stationed no actual troops, thereby filling their minds with suspicion. I ordered Wei Wenchang to lose fifteen engagements in succession to strengthen their confidence. I observed that Coiled Serpent Valley had only one road, that its two walls were bare rock without a tree, and that the ground below was all sand. I therefore ordered Ma Dai to position black, oil-coated chests throughout the valley. Inside those chests were fire-bombs prepared beforehand, called ‘earth-thunder.’ Each bomb contained nine smaller bombs, and they were buried thirty paces apart, with hollowed bamboo poles connecting them to carry the powder fuses; once ignited, they could rend the mountain and split the rocks. I also ordered Zhao Zilong to prepare carts of straw and place them in the valley. And I had great timbers and rocks made ready upon the mountain. Then I ordered Wei Yan to lure Wutugu and the rattan-armored troops into the valley. Once Wei Yan had been allowed out, their way was cut off and they were burned. I have heard it said, ‘What profits by water must suffer by fire.’ Though swords and arrows cannot penetrate the rattan armor, it is soaked in oil and must catch fire when exposed to flame. With the southern troops so obstinate, how could victory have been won without an attack by fire? Yet to leave not one seed of the people of Wuge alive is my great sin!” The generals bowed to the ground and said, “The Prime Minister’s divine calculations are beyond the fathoming of ghosts and gods!” Kongming ordered Meng Huo to be brought before him. Meng Huo knelt below the command tent. Kongming ordered his bonds removed and had him taken to another tent, where wine and food were given him to settle his nerves. Kongming summoned the officer in charge of the wine and food to his couch, gave him secret instructions, and sent him away.

u.src: Kongming returned to camp, took his seat in the command tent, and told his generals, “I resorted to this stratagem only because I had no choice, but it has gravely diminished my store of hidden virtue.
I knew the enemy would expect me to place ambushes where the woods were thick, so I merely displayed banners there and stationed no actual troops, thereby filling their minds with suspicion.
I ordered Wei Wenchang to lose fifteen engagements in succession to strengthen their confidence.

I observed that Coiled Serpent Valley had only one road, that its two walls were bare rock without a tree, and that the ground below was all sand. I therefore ordered Ma Dai to position black, oil-coated chests throughout the valley. Inside those chests were fire-bombs prepared beforehand, called ‘earth-thunder.’ Each bomb contained nine smaller bombs, and they were buried thirty paces apart, with hollowed bamboo poles connecting them to carry the powder fuses;
once ignited, they could rend the mountain and split the rocks.
I also ordered Zhao Zilong to prepare carts of straw and place them in the valley.
And I had great timbers and rocks made ready upon the mountain.
Then I ordered Wei Yan to lure Wutugu and the rattan-armored troops into the valley. Once Wei Yan had been allowed out, their way was cut off and they were burned.
I have heard it said, ‘What profits by water must suffer by fire.’
Though swords and arrows cannot penetrate the rattan armor, it is soaked in oil and must catch fire when exposed to flame.
With the southern troops so obstinate, how could victory have been won without an attack by fire?
Yet to leave not one seed of the people of Wuge alive is my great sin!”
The generals bowed to the ground and said, “The Prime Minister’s divine calculations are beyond the fathoming of ghosts and gods!”
Kongming ordered Meng Huo to be brought before him.
Meng Huo knelt below the command tent.
Kongming ordered his bonds removed and had him taken to another tent, where wine and food were given him to settle his nerves.
Kongming summoned the officer in charge of the wine and food to his couch, gave him secret instructions, and sent him away.

p.src: Meanwhile, Meng Huo, Lady Zhurong, Meng You, the lord of Dailai Cave, and all their clansmen were drinking in the other tent. Suddenly a man entered the tent and told Meng Huo, “The Prime Minister is ashamed to face you and does not wish to see you. He has specially ordered me to release you so that you may return, raise another army, and come again to decide the victory. You should leave at once.” Meng Huo wept and said, “Seven times captured and seven times released—such a thing has never occurred since antiquity. Though I am a man beyond the pale of civilization, I know something of propriety and righteousness. Could I truly be so shameless?” Then, together with his brothers, wife, children, clansmen, and all the rest, he crawled forward and knelt below the command tent. Baring their shoulders, they confessed their guilt and said, “Before the Prime Minister’s heavenly might, the people of the south will never rebel again!” Kongming asked, “Do you submit now?” Meng Huo replied through his tears, “My children and my children’s children shall all be grateful for your life-giving grace, as boundless as heaven and earth. How could we not submit!” Kongming then invited Meng Huo into the command tent, held a banquet in celebration, and appointed him lord of the caves in perpetuity. All the territory that had been seized was returned. Meng Huo’s clansmen and all the southern troops were deeply grateful; they leapt for joy and departed. A later poet wrote in praise of Kongming:

p.src: Chief Clerk Fei Yi came forward to remonstrate: “Prime Minister, you personally led the soldiers deep into this barren region and brought the southern lands to submission; now that the southern king has submitted, why not appoint officials and have them guard the region together with Meng Huo?” Kongming replied, “There are three difficulties in doing so. If outsiders are left here, troops must also remain; but the troops would have no food. That is the first difficulty. The southern people have suffered grievously, and their fathers and elder brothers have been killed. If outsiders were left without troops to protect them, disaster would surely follow. That is the second difficulty. The southern people have repeatedly committed crimes punishable by removal and death and are naturally suspicious. If outsiders remain, they will never trust them. That is the third difficulty. Therefore I shall leave no men here and transport no grain, seeking only that we live together in peace, with no cause for trouble.” Everyone was fully convinced. Thereafter, all the southern lands were grateful for Kongming’s benevolence. They erected shrines to him while he yet lived, offered sacrifices in all four seasons, and called him their loving father; each community sent pearls, gold and jewels, cinnabar lacquer, medicinal materials, plow oxen, and warhorses for the army’s use, and swore never again to rebel. The south was now pacified.

p.src: After Kongming had rewarded the army, he began the return march to Shu and ordered Wei Yan to lead his own command as the vanguard. Just as Wei Yan’s troops reached the Lu River, dark clouds suddenly closed in from every side. A violent gale sprang up over the water, whipping sand into the air and sending stones flying, so that the army could advance no farther. Wei Yan withdrew his troops and reported to Kongming. Kongming therefore summoned Meng Huo and questioned him. Indeed:
